You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
I have a soft spot for unfinished things.

Half-read books with old receipts pressed between the pages. A sweater with one sleeve. The sentence a friend abandons halfway through because they're already laughing at the punchline they haven't said yet. Drafts, sketches, gardens that got a little ambitious in April and gave up by July.

There's something honest about them. A finished thing has to pretend it always knew where it was going. An unfinished thing admits it didn't.

Michelangelo left a series of sculptures called the *Slaves* — figures caught mid-struggle inside the marble, one arm free, the rest still stone. Art historians will tell you about technique and commissions falling through, but I like to stand in front of them (in my head, at least) and think they look more alive than most polished statues. They're not posing. They're becoming.

And we're surrounded by that kind of becoming, if you look for it. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction for over 140 years, cranes as permanent a part of its silhouette as the spires. Siena tried to build a cathedral so big it would swallow the old one, ran out of money and plague years, and left one enormous, elegant wall standing alone. Now people picnic in its shadow. It's not a ruin, exactly. It's a cathedral that decided to be something else.

I think I love it because so much of modern life is weirdly obsessed with completion. Close the rings. Clear the inbox. Finish the season. Reach the end of the feed — as if there is one. Everything wants a checkmark.

But the best parts of a day rarely check anything off. It's the walk that wasn't exercise and wasn't errands, just a walk because the light was doing something interesting on the brick buildings. It's the conversation in a kitchen that drifts from dinner plans to childhood fears to whether ghosts would get bored, and never resolves any of it. It's learning three chords and noodling them badly on a porch for an entire summer instead of ever becoming "a guitarist."

My notebooks are full of ideas that stop mid-thought. A line of dialogue with no speaker. A map of a town that doesn't exist, but I labeled the bakery. A list titled "reasons to learn beekeeping" with only one item: *you get to wear the suit*. At first that felt like failure, all that potential squandered. Now I think of them as seeds with the wrapper still on. Not everything has to germinate on schedule.

Even bread knows this. You mix flour and water and wait, and most of the real work happens when you're not touching it at all. It rises in the quiet. If you keep poking it to check, you ruin the rise.

Maybe people are a little like that. We're constantly interrupting our own rising to ask if we're done yet.

So here's to the unfinished letter you'll probably never send but needed to write. To the language you learned just enough of to order coffee and say thank you like you mean it. To the novel in the drawer, the playlist that's only four songs long but perfect, the friendship that picked back up after two years like it was mid-sentence.

They aren't incomplete because they lack something.

They're open. And open things can still surprise you.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical reflection develops a personal affection for unfinished things into a gentle argument for allowing life to remain open-ended.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, observant, and quietly persuasive, finding tenderness in ordinary remnants: receipts in books, an abandoned sentence, a four-song playlist. Its pathos comes from easing the pressure to finish, improve, or define everything. It invites the reader to see incompletion not as failure but as room for surprise, using images of sculpture, bread, and personal projects to make that invitation feel tangible.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds unfinished objects and experiences, creative process, and the contrast between open-ended becoming and modern life’s appetite for checkmarks and closure. It favors small, intimate examples alongside public landmarks, and repeatedly returns to patience: bread rising undisturbed, ideas waiting to germinate, friendships resuming mid-sentence.

## Evidence line
> There's something honest about them.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the coherent sequence of recurring images gives the reflection a distinctive, sustained emphasis on patience and incompletion.
